name.text: Functions in Real Life — domain restrictions from context (discrete vs continuous)

questiontext.text:
A ticket vendor sells tickets for \({@price@}\) each. If \(n\) tickets are sold, the total revenue is

\[ R(n) = {@price@}n. \]

Which of the following best describes the domain of \(R\) in this real-life context?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]
[[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Although the formula \(R(n)={@price@}n\) is defined algebraically for every real number \(n\), the context restricts what actually makes sense: you can only sell a whole number of tickets, and you cannot sell a negative number of them. So the realistic domain is \(n \in \{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}\), even though the algebraic domain would be all real numbers.

This is a common trap: always check whether the real-world context restricts the domain beyond what the algebra alone would suggest.
